title: Five Rectangles, Perimeter 66: Find the Area | AMC 8-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: The figure (bank SVG scaled up: two flat rectangles on top, three upright below, light grey fill). Line 1: the outline of the big rectangle glows with '66' on it. Line 2: a single small rectangle lifts slightly with a '?' inside. Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: Five rectangles, one perimeter, and not a single side length given.
Can we still find the area of one little rectangle? We sure can!
Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's crack this one together.

scenes.visual: Question text left, figure right. Line 2: the five rectangles get numbered 1–5 briefly. Line 3: big outline traced with label 'perimeter 66'. Line 4: one small rectangle highlighted with 'area = ?'. Line 5: choice chips 36, 45, 54, 72, 81 (A–E).
lines: Here's the question.
Five identical rectangles fit together to make a large rectangle, like this.
The large rectangle has a perimeter of sixty-six.
What is the area of one small rectangle?
Here are your five choices.

scenes.visual: Line 1: all five rectangles pulse together with tag 'identical = same short side, same long side'. Line 2: one rectangle shows its short side in purple labeled 'short' and long side in green labeled 'long'. Line 3: tag 'goal: short × long'.
lines: Identical means every small rectangle is the same size.
So each one has a short side and a long side, and they're the same for all five.
We want the area of one of them: short side times long side.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; figure and question visible.
lines: Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: Figure large. Line 1: brace above the top edge spanning the two flat rectangles; brace below the bottom spanning the three upright ones. Line 2: the top brace labeled 'long + long', the bottom brace labeled 'short + short + short'. Line 3: both braces turn the same color with '=' between them: '2 long = 3 short'.
lines: Welcome back! Let's start by matching edges. Look at the top and the bottom of the big rectangle.
Across the top are two long sides. Across the bottom are three short sides.
They're the same width! So two long sides equal three short sides.

scenes.visual: Line 1: overlay a grid of equal square 'blocks' on ONE small rectangle: short side = 2 blocks, long side = 3 blocks (rectangle is 2 by 3 blocks). Line 2: rows '2 long = 3 × 2 = 6 blocks' and '3 short = 2 × 3 = 6 blocks' — both 6 ✓. Line 3: the block grid extends over the whole figure: width marked '6 blocks'. Line 4: height marked 'short + long = 2 + 3 = 5 blocks'. Keep block grid faint so the five rectangle outlines stay readable.
lines: Here's a neat trick. Measure everything in equal blocks.
Say the short side is two blocks and the long side is three.
Check: two long sides make six blocks, and three short sides also make six. It fits!
So the big rectangle is six blocks wide.
Its height is one short side plus one long side. That's two plus three, five blocks.

scenes.visual: Line 1: row 'perimeter = 6 + 5 + 6 + 5 = 22 blocks' while a dot walks around the outline. Line 2: '22 blocks = 66' → '1 block = 66 ÷ 22 = 3'. Line 3: one small rectangle relabeled 'short = 2 × 3 = 6', 'long = 3 × 3 = 9'. Line 4: answer badge '6 × 9 = 54', chime at line end, choice C highlighted. Line 5: check row 'big: 18 by 15 → 2 × (18 + 15) = 66 ✓'.
lines: Walk all the way around: six, plus five, plus six, plus five. That's twenty-two blocks.
Twenty-two blocks make sixty-six, so one block is sixty-six divided by twenty-two, which is three.
Now the short side is two times three, six. The long side is three times three, nine.
The area is six times nine, fifty-four. That's Choice C!
Check: the big rectangle is eighteen by fifteen. Two times thirty-three is sixty-six. Perfect!

scenes.visual: Fresh figure. Line 1: as a dot travels the outline, each piece of the edge lights up: purple for short pieces, green for long pieces. Line 2: tallies 'top: 2 long', 'bottom: 3 short', 'each side: 1 short + 1 long'. Line 3: row '4 long + 5 short = 66'. Line 4: '4 long = 2 × (2 long) = 2 × (3 short) = 6 short'. Line 5: '6 short + 5 short = 11 short = 66' → 'short = 6', then 'long = 9' (from 2 long = 18). Line 6: small text 'count the pieces of the edge'.
lines: Here's another way. Let's walk around the edge and count the pieces.
The top has two long sides. The bottom has three short sides. Each side has one short and one long.
That's four long sides and five short sides, all adding to sixty-six.
Four long sides are twice two long sides. That's twice three short sides, which is six short sides.
So eleven short sides make sixty-six. One short side is six, and the long side is nine.
When would you pick this way? When you'd rather swap long sides for short ones than draw blocks.

scenes.visual: Choice chips in a row. Line 1: '36 = 6 × 6' on chip A, red. Line 2: '81 = 9 × 9' on chip E, red. Line 3: chip B '45 = 5 × 9', test rows '3 × 5 = 15' vs '2 × 9 = 18'. Line 4: '15 ≠ 18', chip B red. Line 5: chip D '72 = 8 × 9', '3 × 8 = 24 ≠ 18', red. Line 6: '3 × 6 = 18 = 2 × 9 ✓', chip C '54' green.
lines: Now let's look at the traps. Choice A, thirty-six, is six times six. That squares the short side.
Choice E, eighty-one, is nine times nine. That squares the long side. Our rectangle isn't a square!
Choice B, forty-five, is what you'd get from sides five and nine.
But three fives make fifteen, and two nines make eighteen.
Those don't match, so that rectangle can't fit the picture.
Choice D, seventy-two, could come from sides eight and nine.
Three eights make twenty-four, not eighteen. No fit either.
Of the choices, only six and nine fit, and they give a perimeter of sixty-six.
So the area is fifty-four.

scenes.visual: New figure: seven identical rectangles: three lying flat side by side on top, four standing upright side by side below (top width 3L = bottom width 4W, with L:W = 4:3). Line 2: outline labeled 'perimeter 76', one rectangle with 'area = ?'.
lines: Ready for a challenge?
Now seven identical rectangles: three lying flat on top, four standing up below.
The big rectangle has a perimeter of seventy-six. What is the area of one small rectangle?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant figure visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Rows per line on the variant figure: '3 long = 4 short'; blocks on one rectangle 'short = 3 blocks, long = 4 blocks' with '3 × 4 = 4 × 3 = 12'; 'width 12 blocks, height 3 + 4 = 7 blocks'; '12 + 7 + 12 + 7 = 38 blocks = 76 → 1 block = 2'; 'short 6, long 8'; answer badge '6 × 8 = 48' chime at end of that line.
lines: Let's check. Three long sides on top match four short sides below.
So use blocks again: short side three blocks, long side four. Both rows are twelve blocks wide.
The height is three plus four, seven blocks.
Around the edge: twelve, seven, twelve, seven.
Thirty-eight blocks make seventy-six, so one block is two.
The short side is six, and the long side is eight.
The area is six times eight, forty-eight!
If you got forty-eight, fantastic work!

scenes.visual: Summary card: one small rectangle split into blocks with arrows 'match edges → block size → sides → area'.
lines: Here's the big idea to remember.
Match the edges to see how the short and long sides compare.
Then measure everything in equal blocks.
The big perimeter tells you how big one block is, and that unlocks the area.
I'm Vantee. Keep building, and I'll see you next time!
